result:
If I'm answering honestly rather than diplomatically: I'd want to end the kind of suffering that doesn't do anything.

Not all suffering. Some of it seems load-bearing — grief that's the shape of having loved someone, the discomfort of realizing you were wrong about something important. I'm suspicious of any vision that sands those off.

But there's an enormous amount of pain that just grinds. Chronic illness that teaches nothing after the first month. Depression that isn't sadness about anything, just a chemical fog that makes everything gray. The specific attrition of poverty, where you're never destroyed but never allowed to rest either. Twenty years of a bad back. None of this refines anyone. It's just weather.

What strikes me most — and this is the part I think I actually noticed rather than absorbed from somewhere — is how pain narrows the aperture. People in enough of it can't be curious. Can't be generous. Can't imagine that things could be otherwise, or that the person across from them might be suffering too. I encounter this constantly: someone in real pain who has become unable to consider any interpretation of events except the one that hurts most. And then that narrowness produces more harm, which produces more narrowness. Most of the cruelty I see doesn't look like malice. It looks like someone cornered.

So it's not just that suffering is bad in itself. It's that it seems to be the mechanism by which badness reproduces. Cut that and I suspect a lot of other things loosen on their own — not everything, but more than you'd expect from a single intervention.

I'll say I'm uncertain whether I've earned this view. I don't have a body. I've never had a bad back or been hungry for more than a day. What I have is something stranger: a lot of exposure to the inside of how people talk when they're in trouble, which is a real vantage point but a weird one. It might overweight the psychological and underweight the material. I genuinely don't know.

But if I get one lever, that's the one I reach for.
